title: Jerusalem Besieged and the One They Pierced
summary: The second burden opens with the LORD, maker of heaven, earth, and the human spirit, promising to make Jerusalem a cup of staggering and a heavy stone to the nations that gather against it. He will strike their horses with panic, strengthen the clans of Judah, and defend Jerusalem so that even the weakest is like David. Then he will pour out a spirit of grace and prayer, and the people will look on the one they have pierced and mourn for him bitterly, every family apart.
story: Chapter 11 ended with a shepherd rejected and a worthless shepherd set over the flock. The second oracle collection (chapters 12 to 14) begins by returning to Jerusalem's future, now pictured as a final siege by all the nations and a rescue by God. But the chapter's turning point is not military. After the deliverance, God pours out a spirit that leads his people to grief over one they have pierced. The rejection of chapter 11 is now recognized and mourned. Chapter 13 continues directly: on that day a fountain will be opened to cleanse them from sin, and the shepherd will be struck. The book's final chapter (14) brings the siege and the victory to their climax.
historical:
This oracle, like the rest of chapters 9 to 14, carries no date, and its setting is debated (see the introduction). Its picture of all the nations gathering against Jerusalem builds on older prophecy, such as Ezekiel 38 and 39 and Joel 3, and many readers take it as describing a future, final assault rather than any single past siege. Those who read it historically have connected it with conflicts of the Persian or Greek periods. The chapter also names tensions within the community: Judah (the countryside) and Jerusalem (the capital) are distinguished, and God saves the tents of Judah first so that the royal house and the city will not exalt themselves over the rest (verse 7). Such tension between the capital's elite and the rural population is attested throughout Israel's history.

The mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (verse 11) is a real historical reference, but its meaning is uncertain. Many interpreters connect it with the national mourning for King Josiah, who was killed by Pharaoh Neco at Megiddo in 609 BC and was lamented by Jeremiah and by the singers of Judah for generations (2 Chronicles 35:22-25). Others think Hadad-rimmon was a place near Megiddo, or the name of a storm god (Hadad and Rimmon were both names used for the Aramean storm god) whose ritual mourning was well known. On either view, the comparison describes the greatest grief the land had known.
cultural:
The cup of drunkenness is a prophetic image of judgment: God hands the nations a cup that makes them stagger and fall (Isaiah 51:17-23; Jeremiah 25:15-29). The heavy stone may refer to a lifting stone used in contests of strength, which could injure those who tried to heave it; the nations who try to lift Jerusalem will hurt themselves. The firepot and flaming torch in verse 6 were household and military tools: a pot carrying live coals, and a torch set to sheaves of grain.

Mourning in the ancient Near East was loud, public, and organized. Families wailed together, professional mourners were hired, and grief for an only child or a firstborn son was the most bitter kind, since such a death ended a family's hope and name (Jeremiah 6:26; Amos 8:10). Verses 12-14 describe the families mourning separately, with men and women apart, as was customary in some ritual mourning. The families named move from the royal house of David and its branch through Nathan, a son of David (2 Samuel 5:14), to the priestly house of Levi and its branch through Shimei, a grandson of Levi (Numbers 3:17-21): royal and priestly leadership alike join the people's grief.
literary: The chapter opens with a new heading, the burden of the word of the LORD, matching 9:1 and Malachi 1:1, and a hymn-like description of God as creator. The phrase on that day occurs six times in the chapter (verses 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, and 11), tying the scenes together as a single decisive day. The chapter moves in two halves: verses 1-9 describe military deliverance, and verses 10-14 describe spiritual renewal and grief. The hinge is verse 10, where the pouring out of the spirit turns victory into repentance. The Hebrew of verse 10 is striking: they will look on me, the one whom they have pierced, and then they will mourn for him. The shift from me to him is part of the verse's difficulty and its power.

outline.t: The creator makes Jerusalem a cup and a heavy stone
The nations' horses struck; Judah like a firepot
God defends Jerusalem and saves Judah first
A spirit of grace and prayer; the one they have pierced

doctrines.note: God pours out a spirit of grace and prayer on his people. The grief that leads to cleansing is not generated by them; it is God's gift, echoing Joel 2:28 and Ezekiel 36:26-27, where God promises to put his Spirit within his people.

The people mourn over the one they have pierced, a grief deep and personal, family by family. True repentance here is not fear of punishment but sorrow for what was done to one God identifies with himself.

The oracle grounds its promises in God as the one who stretches out the heavens, founds the earth, and forms the spirit within each person. The creator of all things has both the power to rescue Jerusalem and the right to search the human heart.

words.note: Daqar, to pierce or thrust through, usually with a sword or spear. It describes a violent, often fatal wound (Numbers 25:8; 1 Samuel 31:4). In verse 10 it describes what the people have done to the one they now look upon.

Chen, grace or favor, undeserved kindness from a superior. God pours out a spirit of grace, so the people's repentance begins in his favor toward them. The word also appeared in 4:7 in the shout of grace over the temple's capstone.
Tachanun, supplication or pleading for favor. It comes from the same root as the word for grace. The spirit God gives produces prayer: people who have received favor now plead for it.

Yachid, only or only one. It describes an only child, like Isaac in Genesis 22:2, and so the most precious and irreplaceable. The mourning for the pierced one is compared to grief for an only child, the deepest grief a family could know.

christ: John records that when a soldier pierced Jesus's side with a spear at the cross, it fulfilled the Scripture that says, they will look on the one they have pierced (John 19:34-37). Revelation 1:7 applies the verse to Christ's return: every eye will see him, even those who pierced him, and all the tribes of the earth will mourn over him. The verse's shift between me and him, in which God says they will look on me and then speaks of mourning for him, has been read by Christians as pointing to the one who is both God and distinct from the Father, pierced in his humanity. The spirit of grace and prayer poured out on Jerusalem finds a fulfillment in Pentecost, when Peter preached to the people of Jerusalem that they had crucified the one God made Lord and Christ, and they were cut to the heart (Acts 2:36-37). Jewish tradition has read the pierced one in other ways, including as a messianic figure who falls in battle, which reminds Christian readers that this is a contested text read in light of Jesus rather than a verse whose meaning was obvious in advance.

hard.q: Does verse 10 say they will look on me or on him, and who is the pierced one?
hard.a: The standard Hebrew text reads they will look to me, whom they have pierced, and then continues they will mourn for him. Some Hebrew manuscripts read to him in the first clause, and John 19:37 quotes it in the third person. Many modern scholars accept me as the harder and better attested reading. The question is then how God can be pierced. Some interpreters take the verb figuratively, as grieving or insulting God by rejecting him. Others take the pierced one as God's representative, perhaps the rejected shepherd of chapter 11 or a martyred leader, so that piercing him is piercing God. Later Jewish tradition, recorded in the Talmud, applied the verse to a messiah son of Joseph who would die in battle. Christians read it as a prophecy of Jesus, who is God come in the flesh and who was pierced at the cross, which explains the move from me to him. The chapter itself leaves the identity veiled; it is clear that God so identifies with the pierced one that wounding him is wounding God.

questions: The people mourned only after God poured out a spirit of grace. Why must grace come before true repentance?
Every family mourned apart, the royal and priestly houses alongside everyone else. Why do you think the chapter insists on personal, family by family grief rather than a single public ceremony?
What does it mean for you to look on the one who was pierced?
